> **Note:** Everything in this article is about the default `"pjrt"` backend, running on its CUDA plugin.

Here, we show how to use a custom CUDA kernel in {anvl}.
Read the [Custom Calls](custom_calls.html) article first if you haven't already.

The structure of this article is as follows:

1. Writing the CUDA kernel
2. Writing the handler that launches it
3. Building both
4. Registering both with {pjrt}

## Step 1: Write the kernel

We split the code into two files: the kernel goes into a `.cu` (CUDA) file compiled by `nvcc` (the NVIDIA CUDA compiler), and the FFI handler into a `.cpp` file.
We start by implementing the CUDA kernel for the element-wise `hypot()` operation.


```cu
// hypot_kernel.cu -- compiled by nvcc
#include <cuda_runtime.h>

template <typename T>
__global__ void hypot_kernel(const T *x, const T *y, T *out, size_t n) {
  size_t i = blockIdx.x * static_cast<size_t>(blockDim.x) + threadIdx.x;
  if (i < n) out[i] = hypot(x[i], y[i]);
}
```

The launcher starts the kernel on the given stream and returns `NULL` on success, and CUDA's description of the error otherwise.
The handler returns as soon as the kernel is enqueued, so this check is the only way to report a failed launch; without it, the error only surfaces, unrelated, at the next CUDA call.

```cu
template <typename T>
static const char *launch(void *stream, const T *x, const T *y, T *out,
                          size_t n) {
  if (n == 0) return nullptr;  // a launch of zero blocks is itself an error
  const int threads = 256;
  const int blocks = static_cast<int>((n + threads - 1) / threads);
  hypot_kernel<T><<<blocks, threads, 0, static_cast<cudaStream_t>(stream)>>>(
      x, y, out, n);
  cudaError_t err = cudaGetLastError();
  return err == cudaSuccess ? nullptr : cudaGetErrorString(err);
}
```

The handler in the `.cpp` file reaches the kernel through launchers declared `extern "C"`, which gives them plain C symbol names instead of compiler-specific mangled C++ ones, so that the two files, compiled separately and possibly by different compilers, find each other when they are linked.
Because an `extern "C"` function cannot be a template, the `.cu` file exposes one launcher per supported data type:

```cu
extern "C" const char *mypkg_launch_hypot_f32(void *stream, const float *x,
                                              const float *y, float *out,
                                              size_t n) {
  return launch<float>(stream, x, y, out, n);
}

extern "C" const char *mypkg_launch_hypot_f64(void *stream, const double *x,
                                              const double *y, double *out,
                                              size_t n) {
  return launch<double>(stream, x, y, out, n);
}
```

## Step 2: Write the handler

The handler checks its operands as the CPU handler does, but instead of looping over the elements itself, it passes their pointers to the launcher.
These are *device* pointers, which only the kernel may dereference: as XLA's [custom call guide](https://openxla.org/xla/custom_call) points out, the handler itself still runs on the CPU.

```c++
// hypot_cuda.cpp -- compiled by R's C++ toolchain, no CUDA headers
// [[Rcpp::plugins(cpp20)]]
// [[Rcpp::depends(pjrt)]]
#include <Rcpp.h>
#include <string>
#include "xla/ffi/api/ffi.h"

using namespace xla::ffi;

extern "C" const char *mypkg_launch_hypot_f32(void *stream, const float *x,
                                              const float *y, float *out,
                                              size_t n);
extern "C" const char *mypkg_launch_hypot_f64(void *stream, const double *x,
                                              const double *y, double *out,
                                              size_t n);

static Error do_hypot_cuda(void *stream, AnyBuffer x, AnyBuffer y,
                           Result<AnyBuffer> out) {
  size_t n = out->element_count();
  if (x.element_count() != n || y.element_count() != n) {
    return Error::InvalidArgument("hypot: operands must have the same size");
  }
  DataType dt = x.element_type();
  if (y.element_type() != dt || out->element_type() != dt) {
    return Error::InvalidArgument("hypot: operands and result must have the "
                                  "same dtype");
  }
  const char *err = nullptr;
  switch (dt) {
    case DataType::F32:
      err = mypkg_launch_hypot_f32(stream, x.typed_data<float>(),
                                   y.typed_data<float>(),
                                   out->typed_data<float>(), n);
      break;
    case DataType::F64:
      err = mypkg_launch_hypot_f64(stream, x.typed_data<double>(),
                                   y.typed_data<double>(),
                                   out->typed_data<double>(), n);
      break;
    default:
      return Error::InvalidArgument("hypot: only f32 and f64 are supported");
  }
  if (err != nullptr) return Error::Internal(std::string("hypot: ") + err);
  return Error::Success();
}
```

Compared to the CPU handler, the binding specification gains one entry: `.Ctx<PlatformStream<void *>>()` passes the CUDA stream on which XLA dispatched the operation, in front of the buffers.
Everything the handler enqueues must go on that stream.
As for the CPU handler, a getter hands the handler to R:

```c++
XLA_FFI_DEFINE_HANDLER_EXPLICIT(hypot_handler_cuda, do_hypot_cuda,
                                Ffi::Bind()
                                    .Ctx<PlatformStream<void *>>()
                                    .Arg<AnyBuffer>()
                                    .Arg<AnyBuffer>()
                                    .Ret<AnyBuffer>());

// [[Rcpp::export]]
SEXP hypot_handler_cuda_ptr() {
  return R_MakeExternalPtr((void *)hypot_handler_cuda, R_NilValue, R_NilValue);
}
```

## Step 3: Build both

We do not need a system CUDA toolkit for this.
On a machine with an NVIDIA GPU, `pjrt::install_pjrt()` installs the [{pjrt.cuda}](https://github.com/r-xla/pjrt.cuda) package along with the CUDA plugin, and {pjrt.cuda} provides the CUDA toolkit: `nvcc` (the NVIDIA CUDA Compiler), the CUDA headers, and the CUDA runtime library, whose locations `pjrt.cuda::bin_path()`, `pjrt.cuda::include_path()` and `pjrt.cuda::lib_path()` report.
{pjrt.cuda} is Linux only, as is the CUDA plugin.

With these, `nvcc` compiles the kernel into an object file, and `Rcpp::sourceCpp()` compiles the handler as in the CPU article, linking the kernel and the CUDA runtime library into it through the `PKG_LIBS` environment variable.

## Step 4: Register both

Finally, we register both handlers under the same target, in place of the CPU-only registration of the CPU article:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
pjrt::pjrt_register_custom_call(
  "mypkg_hypot",
  list(cpu = hypot_handler_ptr(), cuda = hypot_handler_cuda_ptr())
)
```

## Using in a package

Offering a custom CUDA kernel comes with various considerations.
The core problems are that:

1. CRAN's machines do not have a CUDA toolkit and {pjrt.cuda} cannot be installed there because it downloads the CUDA toolkit at installation time.
2. Not every user has an NVIDIA GPU.

While we hope to offer a more structured solution to this in the future, a currently practical approach is to compile the CUDA code at run time, either in the package's `.onLoad` hook (e.g., conditioned on {pjrt.cuda} being installed) or when the function that requires the CUDA kernel is first called.
Only the kernel has to be compiled at run time: the handler includes no CUDA header, so it is compiled with the package, like the CPU handler.
As the launchers do not exist yet when the package is installed, the handler cannot be linked against them; instead, the package compiles the `.cu` file with `nvcc -shared` into a shared library, loads it with `dyn.load()`, and hands the addresses of the launchers to the handler as function pointers.
Compiled into a temporary directory, the kernel has to be recompiled in every new R session; keeping the library in a persistent directory such as `tools::R_user_dir("mypkg", "cache")` compiles it only once.
Instead of `nvcc`, a package can also use [NVRTC](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/nvrtc/) (the NVIDIA Runtime Compiler), which {pjrt.cuda} ships too, to compile the kernel from a string at run time, and then load and launch it through the CUDA driver API.
